newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Japan stocks likely to waver.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Japan stocks likely to waver.

text.p: Japan stocks are likely to waver this week as the market consolidates after its best gains of the year, brokers said.

"After the Nikkei average hit a 1997 calendar year high (of 20,910.79) on June 26, consolidation moves have strengthened, much like in the previous year," a managing director at a middle-sized brokerage said.
"Without the emergence of aggressive buyers, the Nikkei average could weaken further."
Last year, the Nikkei's highest close was 22,666.80 on June 26.
Brokers said the focus would be on the activity of foreign investors, which has slowed after the end-June book closing.
Pension funds were also waiting for a chance to bargain-hunt, but the Nikkei 225 still had a way to go before such moves would emerge, they said.

"Pensions have been buying actively lately and are in no hurry to buy more, especially since the Nikkei average is consolidating," a "Big Four" broker said. "Investors will start fishing at the bottom when the Nikkei falls into the 19,700-19,900 range," he added.
Brokers said they saw a range of 19,500 to 20,400 for the Nikkei average this week.
Market sources said that the cautious market mood, which has caused turnover to shrivel to 300 million shares, was partly due to a lack of evidence that Japan's economy was recovering strongly.
They said the scandal at Nomura Securities Co Ltd, which is showing signs of spreading, was also hanging heavily over the market.

The racketeer involved in the scandal has said that the other Big Four brokerages, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd , Nikko Securities Co Ltd and Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd had conducted illegal stock deals for him.

Adding to the uncertainty was a newspaper report that Nomura had been quizzed by prosecutors about dubious transfers of a major loan firm's shares to politicians and government officials prior to its initial public offering.
Japan's biggest consumer finance firm, Takefuji Corp, said it was probably the loan company mentioned in the report.
"Investors are extremely reluctant to move with the future unclear," said Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities general manager.
News on Friday that construction firm Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd had decided to apply for court protection with debts of 511 billion yen, further soured the market mood, brokers said.
The Nikkei average ended Friday 153.41 points or 0.76 percent lower at 19,968.00, recovering from an intra-day low of 19,907.39.
It ended below 20,000 for the first time since May 27 when it finished at 19,889.89.
"In the short term, the market may be pressured by Tokai, but the sooner ailing firms are cleaned up, the faster the industry will recover," said Mitsuru Hayashino, Sanyo Securities general manager.
